summary: For ages 5–7: help children describe the multi-sensory experience of being INSIDE a rainforest — hot and sticky (humid), dark on the forest floor, loud with animal and insect calls, and dripping with water — and crucially pair each sensation to a cause the child can grasp (dark BECAUSE tall trees block the light; sticky BECAUSE the air is full of water; loud BECAUSE hundreds of hidden animals call; dripping BECAUSE rain and dew run off millions of leaves). This is descriptive natural history for KS1/early-years, not mechanism. The core activity is a rich sensory exploration (ideally a cutaway image of the forest interior with an ambient soundscape); supporting activities include a canopy-light scaffold, embodied acting-out, and an end-of-topic recall check.
misconceptions: 'A forest is bright and open' — children picture a sunny park; the rainforest floor is actually dim because the canopy intercepts the light.
'Rainforests are only wet when it's raining' — the air stays sticky/humid and leaves drip even between showers.
'Hot places are dry like a desert' — conflating hot with dry; rainforests are hot AND wet.
'It's quiet like a library in the forest' — in fact it is loud with animal and insect sound.

activities.title: Explore inside the rainforest: sensation and its cause
steps: Look at a cutaway picture of the rainforest interior showing the bright, dense treetops above and the dim forest floor below.

For each part of the scene, say what it would FEEL, SOUND or LOOK like, then say WHY: tap/point to the treetops and answer 'Why is it so dark down on the ground?' (the tall trees catch the sunlight first, like a leafy umbrella).
Point to the sticky air and say what causes it (the air is full of water — that's why you feel sweaty/damp).
Point to a hidden bird or insect and describe the loud calls, then say why (hundreds of hidden animals calling at once).
Point to a glistening leaf and describe the dripping, then say why (rain and dew running off millions of leaves).
If an ambient soundscape is available (bird calls, insect buzz, dripping water), listen to it so 'loud' is heard, not just read.
activities.insight: The gloom, stickiness and noise inside a rainforest are not random — each sensation has a cause: thick, tall treetops block the light, warm air full of water from heavy rain feels sticky, and many hidden animals call. The child builds an explanation (cause), not just a description.

activities.title: Light through the canopy: fewer or more leaves
steps: Look at a picture of the forest floor beneath the treetops.
Imagine (or, if a slider/control is available, adjust) the number of leaves in the canopy: with more leaves overhead, watch the floor get darker; with fewer leaves, watch it get brighter.
Say in your own words why a thick, leafy canopy makes the ground dark.
activities.insight: The darkness of the forest floor depends on how much light the treetops catch first — more leaves overhead means less light reaching the ground.

activities.title: Act it out and compare with a familiar place
steps: Fan yourself to show the hot, sticky air; cup an ear to listen for the animal calls; flick fingers down to show the dripping leaves.
Compare the rainforest with a place you know — a local wood, a park, or your bedroom. Which is hotter? Which is darker on the ground? Which is noisier? Which is wetter?
Say one thing that is different about the rainforest and why.
activities.insight: Contrasting the rainforest with a familiar place makes 'hot, dark, loud, wet' felt rather than abstract, and embodying each sensation aids recall.

activities.title: End check: match each sense to its cause
steps: Match each sensation to its reason: sticky air → the air is full of water; dark floor → the tall trees block the light; loud → many hidden animals calling; dripping → rain and dew running off the leaves.
Answer: Why is the forest floor dark even in the daytime?
Name two sounds you would hear inside a rainforest.
activities.insight: Check that the child can recall both the sensations and the cause of each, especially the canopy explanation for the dark floor.

checkQuestion: Imagine walking into a rainforest. Would the air feel hot and sticky or cool and dry, and would it be quiet or noisy down on the ground? Tell me what it's like, and then tell me WHY the ground is so dark.
checkAnswer: The air feels hot and sticky (humid) and it's very noisy — full of bird calls, insect buzzing and dripping water. Down on the ground it's dark even in the daytime, because the tall trees and thick canopy block most of the sunlight before it reaches the floor.
